title: Gideon and the Summer
premise: Xanthe Hartwell's struggling café gets an unexpected lifeline when Gideon Marsh — her estranged childhood friend turned hotelier — offers a business deal wrapped in a lie: pose as his girlfriend at his family's summer reunion to secure an inheritance contingent on his settling down. What begins as mutual convenience deepens over one long coastal summer of shared kitchens, old wounds, and family secrets about why they truly fell apart years ago. When Xanthe discovers the inheritance clause was fabricated by Gideon's scheming aunt to force him home, and that taking the deal would mean selling her café block to developers anyway, she walks away. In the end, Gideon forfeits the inheritance, buys the café himself as her landlord-turned-partner, and asks for a real first date — proving second chances belong to people brave enough to claim them.
about_author: Odile Delacroix is the pen name of a former line cook who spent a decade writing love stories on the backs of order tickets before turning to fiction full-time. She lives in a seaside town much like the one in this book, where she still judges cafés by their lemon tarts.

chapters.title: Three Missed Payments
chapters.summary: Xanthe's POV. A final notice arrives at Butter & Salt Café on the morning of its best sales day, and Xanthe calculates exactly how many lemon tarts stand between her and ruin. The beat is quiet desperation masked by competence.

chapters.title: The Man at Table Four
chapters.summary: Gideon's POV. Gideon returns to Hartwell's Point after nine years abroad, nursing cold coffee and older regrets, and recognizes Xanthe before she recognizes him. The beat is the ache of coming home to a place that remembers what you did.

chapters.title: An Offer With Crumbs On It
chapters.summary: Xanthe's POV. Gideon proposes the fake-relationship arrangement: accompany him to the Marsh family reunion, and he'll cover her debts through autumn. She refuses on principle, then finds the eviction warning taped to her register. The beat is pride colliding with arithmetic.

chapters.title: Terms and Conditions
chapters.summary: Dual POV. Over closing-time wine, they negotiate rules: no real feelings, no questions about the past, hand-holding permitted. Both are lying to themselves already. The beat is playful tension with fault lines showing.

chapters.title: Arrivals
chapters.summary: Xanthe's POV. The Marsh estate on Cliffmere Bay swallows them whole — cousins, cameras, and Gideon's imperious Aunt Rosalind, who scrutinizes Xanthe like a recipe missing an ingredient. The beat is impostor syndrome in a designer dress.

chapters.title: The First Lie Tastes Sweet
chapters.summary: Gideon's POV. Xanthe improvises their meet-cute so convincingly that Gideon forgets it's fiction, and his grandmother — sharp-eyed, dying, delighted — blesses the match. The beat is the dangerous pleasure of being believed.

chapters.title: What Happened at the Boathouse
chapters.summary: Xanthe's POV. A cousin's drunken toast references 'the boathouse incident,' and Xanthe realizes Gideon left town because of something she never knew. He deflects; she remembers rule two. The beat is suspicion dressed as patience.

chapters.title: Flour, Salt, Midnight
chapters.summary: Dual POV. Escaping the reunion, they bake together in the estate kitchen at midnight — her hands, his terrible knife skills — and talk around the truth until dawn. The beat is intimacy arriving sideways, through work.

chapters.title: Rosalind's Ledger
chapters.summary: Gideon's POV. Gideon catches Aunt Rosalind reviewing documents about the café block and assumes she's vetting Xanthe; readers see she's planning something else. The beat is dramatic irony tightening like a ratchet.

chapters.title: The Summer Fair
chapters.summary: Xanthe's POV. At the town fair, Gideon wins her a ridiculous prize and kisses her in front of everyone — off-script, unforced, real. That night neither invokes rule one. The beat is the fake relationship quietly expiring.

chapters.title: Grandmother's Confession
chapters.summary: Gideon's POV. His grandmother reveals the inheritance clause requiring him to be 'settled' was her invention, meant to drag him home — and hints Rosalind has plans for the Hartwell property. The beat is grief braided with urgency.

chapters.title: Nine Years Ago
chapters.summary: Flashback chapter, dual POV. The boathouse truth surfaces: teenage Gideon, drunk and terrified of leaving, told Xanthe he'd stay for her — then let her believe she wasn't enough to keep him. The beat is old hurt reframed as misunderstanding.

chapters.title: Too Real by Dessert
chapters.summary: Xanthe's POV. At the reunion's final dinner, asked to toast their 'engagement,' Xanthe freezes — because she wants it to be true, and wanting it makes the lie unforgivable. She flees mid-dessert. The beat is panic as self-knowledge.

chapters.title: The Clause
chapters.summary: Gideon's POV. Gideon confronts Rosalind and learns the development deal for the café block predates everything — his return, the reunion, possibly Xanthe herself as collateral. The beat is betrayal rearranging every kindness into evidence.

chapters.title: Reading the Fine Print
chapters.summary: Xanthe's POV. A lawyer's letter reaches the café: signing Gideon's debt relief contract includes a quiet easement ceding her building to Marsh Developments. Whether he knew or not, she can't tell. The beat is heartbreak choosing caution.

chapters.title: The Argument in the Rain
chapters.summary: Dual POV. Gideon comes to explain; Xanthe refuses to be anyone's acquisition. He says 'I chose you'; she says 'You chose the plan first.' He leaves without denying the signature. The beat is both of them right and ruined.

chapters.title: Empty Kitchen
chapters.summary: Xanthe's POV. Packing crates, cancelled orders, and a last batch of lemon tarts nobody orders. Her mother's old recipe card falls out of a drawer — inheritance of a different kind. The beat is grief finding its floor.

chapters.title: The Funeral and the Will
chapters.summary: Gideon's POV. His grandmother dies; the will disinherits anyone who signs Rosalind's development papers and leaves Gideon only a letter: 'Build something that feeds people.' The beat is permission disguised as loss.

chapters.title: Forfeiture
chapters.summary: Gideon's POV. Gideon publicly tears up the inheritance agreement at the reading, resigns from the family firm, and drives through the night to a dark café with a FOR LEASE sign. The beat is a man finally paying full price.

chapters.title: Landlord, Partner, Idiot
chapters.summary: Xanthe's POV. Gideon presents new paperwork: he owns the building now, rent-free for a year, and wants a job — dishwasher, delivery boy, anything — plus one real date, no script. The beat is forgiveness negotiated over flour.

chapters.title: The Real First Date
chapters.summary: Dual POV. They close the café early, eat burnt tarts on the pier where they met as children, and say the true version of everything — the boathouse, the fear, the wanting. The beat is tenderness after wreckage.

chapters.title: Butter & Salt, Reopened
chapters.summary: Epilogue, alternating POVs. One year later: the café thrives, Rosalind's development died with the clause, and a small brass plaque reads 'Est. twice.' Gideon proposes with a ring baked inside a lemon tart. The beat is second chances, claimed on time.
